Although pre-trained language models (PLMs) have achieved remarkable success across numerous tasks, their effectiveness often diminishes when applied to new domains or specific objectives. To address this, numerous adaptation strategies have emerged, yet most rely on extensive pre-training data and fail to adequately handle objective-centric adaptation. This paper introduces Adaptor, a framework designed to adapt PLMs for diverse objectives using only minimal data. Adaptor operates in two stages: first, it identifies the most relevant pre-trained representations for a specific task by learning task-aware adapters; second, it utilizes these adapters to fine-tune the PLM for the target objective. By employing a novel objective-aware objective loss function, Adaptor effectively manages multi-task scenarios. Comprehensive experiments on diverse PLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that Adaptor achieves state-of-the-art performance in both single-task and multi-task settings.

This work introduces the inaugural large-scale, global Mapillary Traffic Sign Dataset, which comprises 1.2 million images covering 40 sign categories from 60 global cities. The data includes detailed annotations for 40 classes, with 1.2 million total images sourced from a worldwide scale. The paper details sign annotation protocols, examines class distribution, and evaluates the dataset's effectiveness through object detection and multi-label classification experiments. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/mapillary/image-datasets/tree/master/mapillary-traffic-sign-dataset.

Collaborative filtering (CF) is a foundational technique in recommender systems, yet it often struggles with data sparsity and the absence of user-item interactions. To address these challenges, self-supervised collaborative filtering (SCF) has emerged as a key area of research. While recent SCF methods have shown promise, they typically rely on extensive hyperparameter tuning and are limited to specific recommendation tasks. In this paper, we introduce a streamlined and efficient framework for SCF that overcomes these limitations. Our approach utilizes a self-supervised task to generate pseudo-positive samples, which are then utilized to pre-train a matrix factorization model. Furthermore, we develop a novel fine-tuning strategy designed to enhance the model's generalization capabilities. Comprehensive experiments across four diverse recommendation datasets demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SCF methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenruiZhang/SelfCF.

This article examines the Tevelev degrees of the $\mathbb{P}^1$, a concept defined by counting the number of Hurwitz covers satisfying specific boundary conditions. By leveraging a recursive method for these calculations, the authors establish that these degrees are generally positive integers.

We introduce a three-dimensional gapped Dirac semimetal featuring mixed dispersive profiles, combining linear and parabolic dynamics. This system is defined by a $2+1$-dimensional $U(1)$ quantum field theory with a $Z_2$ symmetry, incorporating a single $Z_2$-odd Dirac fermion. The resulting low-energy effective theory is a $3+1$-dimensional $Z_2$-invariant quantum electrodynamics. We demonstrate that this model is non-perturbatively renormalizable, with its renormalized effective action derived via the background field method. Furthermore, we analyze the model's phase diagram, identifying a region of strong coupling where the fermion mass is generated through dynamical symmetry breaking.

Let $C$ be a smooth projective curve of genus $g$ over a field $K$ of characteristic zero. We define a curve $D$ as semi-stable when it is reduced and possesses only singular points of type $\mathbb{A}_1$. We define a curve $C$ as slowly moving relative to $D$ if the $\mathfrak{m}_P$-adic valuation of the discriminant of $D-C$ at every point $P \in D$ is at least 2. This paper establishes that for $g \geq 2$, a slowly moving curve $C$ on a semi-stable curve $D$ admits a proper closure $\bar{C}$ within the semi-stable reduction $\bar{D}$ of $D$, such that the intersection number $\bar{C} \cdot \bar{D}$ is at most 4.

Gravitational wave signals from spinning black holes can exhibit higher-order modes (HOMs) that are detectable by ground-based interferometers. This study examines the detectability of these HOMs using the third-generation GW detector network, LIGO, Virgo, and Cosmic Explorer (CE). We introduce a novel, computationally efficient method to estimate the HOM signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) that is independent of the specific waveform model employed. This approach utilizes the signal-to-noise ratio of the quadrupolar mode ($\rho_2$) and the signal-to-noisenoise ratio of the difference between the total S/N and the quadrupolar mode S/N ($\rho_{\rm diff}$). We demonstrate that the ratio of the total S/N to the quadrupolar mode S/N ($\rho_2/\rho_{diff}$) is a nearly constant value, allowing for a precise estimation of the total S/N. Furthermore, we analyze the distribution of the ratio of the total S/N to the quadrupolar mode S/N ($\rho_2/\rho_{diff}$) and the ratio of the total S/N to the quadrupolar mode S/N ($\rho_2/\rho_{diff}$) to determine the probability of detecting HOMs. We find that the probability of detecting HOMs is approximately 0.000000000000000000000000

This study investigates the astrometric detection of dark companions orbiting stars within the Gaia mission's field of view. We demonstrate that even for stars with Gaia EDR3 parallax uncertainties as high as 10%, it is feasible to identify dark companions with masses comparable to or less than those of their host stars, provided the orbits are extensive (with periods exceeding 100 years) and the mass ratio is at least 0.1. We introduce a novel method to detect such systems by analyzing the curvature of the astrometric orbit, which is particularly effective for stars exhibiting parallax uncertainties below 10%. Furthermore, we outline a practical approach for estimating the mass of a dark companion by combining astrometric measurements with the star's luminosity and the companion's assumed mass-luminosity relationship. We also quantify the impact of a dark companion on the measured proper motion of the host star. Finally, we present a comprehensive formula for calculating the astrometric signature of a dark companion, which is valid for both full and partial orbital coverage.

The genetic algorithm (GA) is a widely recognized evolutionary computation technique that has proven effective in solving various optimization problems. This study evaluates the performance of different GA components, specifically focusing on the impact of varied crossover and selection strategies on convergence rates for the 0/1 Knapsack problem. A thorough examination of these methods was conducted using a comprehensive GA framework. The results indicate that the performance of GA is significantly contingent upon the specific choices of crossover and selection operators. Ultimately, empirical evidence suggests that uniform crossover combined with uniform selection yields the fastest convergence for addressing the Knapsack problem.

This work investigates $L^2$-bounds for trilinear oscillatory integrals of a convolution type in two dimensions. Specifically, we establish that when the phase function $\phi$ exhibits nondegenerate Hessian matrix at a critical point, the corresponding operator norm is bounded by a constant independent of the amplitude parameter $|\lambda|$.

This study introduces a hate speech detection system that integrates data augmentation with an ensemble of diverse models. The authors evaluate T5, a text-to-text transformer, employing various strategies to augment data, including paraphrasing and the generation of synthetic negative labels. The findings indicate that combining multiple models yields superior performance compared to relying on a single approach. Additionally, the authors release the project's code and datasets as an open resource.

We examine the scaling behavior of forces derived from valence full configuration interaction quantum Monte Carlo (VFCIQMC) within a model system of 16O, utilizing a basis set constructed from Slater determinants. Our findings indicate that the computational cost associated with calculating these forces increases linearly with respect to the number of VFCIQMC Slater determinants. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the efficiency of this approach can be enhanced by employing a more compact basis of Slater determinants.

Elections are pivotal to democratic societies, yet recent elections have been marred by widespread claims of fraud. Although the majority of these allegations lack factual basis, their prevalence can still influence public opinion and behavior. To address this, we introduce the VoterFraud2020 dataset, which comprises over 1.5 million tweets containing 1.5 million claims of election fraud. These claims are categorized into 14 distinct types, including narratives, assertions, and calls to action. The dataset further includes a comprehensive collection of verified ground truth data regarding whether these claims are false, valid, or lack evidence. This resource offers a detailed analysis of claim distribution across various metrics, such as temporal patterns, engagement levels, and specific claim types. Furthermore, the dataset provides a foundation for developing automated systems to detect and verify election fraud, aiming to enhance the integrity of the electoral process.

This paper establishes that for diffeomorphisms exhibiting non-zero Lyapunov exponents, sublevel sets of the equilibrium state defined by a H\"older function $f$ approach the set of generic vectors as the tolerance $\varepsilon \to 0$. This finding extends a previous result by Dolgopyat, Klein, and Tzvetkov, originally proven for Axiom A attractors, to a broader context. As a consequence, we demonstrate that for such diffeomorphisms, the set of $C^{1+\varepsilon}$ perturbations maintaining hyperbolicity at every point is dense. Furthermore, we prove that within this framework, hyperbolic periodic points in $C^{1+\varepsilon}$ perturbations form a hyperbolic $C^{1}$-dense collection.

Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) are increasingly recognized as a robust approach for quantifying uncertainty in machine learning. However, the high computational cost associated with Bayesian inference has hindered their application to large-scale datasets. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel method for encoding BNN parameters and gradients within a compact latent space. This encoding enables the training of a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to learn a low-dimensional latent posterior distribution. By utilizing a VAE-BNN framework, we can perform inference on this latent distribution, significantly reducing the computational burden of Bayesian training. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the learned latent posterior can be efficiently stored and reused to train BNNs on new tasks without re-executing the full inference process. Our experimental results indicate that this approach yields competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods while achieving substantial reductions in both training time and memory consumption.

This work introduces a semiclassical instanton framework for Marcus–Levich–Jortner (MLJ) electron transfer theory. By applying the instanton method to the MLJ action, we demonstrate that the instanton partition function can be expressed as a sum over individual instanton trajectories. This formulation yields a semiclassical rate expression that remains consistent with the original MLF theory. Furthermore, we analyze the specific characteristics of instanton trajectories within the MLJ model and examine how the number of such trajectories varies in relation to the reorganization energy.

This study introduces a hybrid approach for designing trajectory control systems, which integrates a trajectory planner with a real-time controller. This method is particularly valuable for scenarios involving trajectory modifications, such as when obstacles are detected. By utilizing a controller based on Model Predictive Control (MPC) with constraints, the system can prioritize safety and comfort while ensuring the robot tracks the original path. The authors demonstrate the method's effectiveness through a simulation of a mobile robot navigating a dynamic environment.

The substantial spin Seebeck effect observed in thin-film Heusler alloys is investigated through a magnon drag framework. This mechanism attributes the effect to the transfer of momentum from an applied temperature gradient to magnetic excitations, resulting in the generation of a spin current. The analysis indicates that the thermoelectric response is highly sensitive to the specific characteristics of magnetic excitations, particularly the density of states near the Fermi level. Furthermore, the proposed model elucidates the temperature dependence of such effects and establishes a connection between the magnitude of these responses and the material's magnetic ordering temperature.

This paper investigates the "Perfect Sum" problem, a recently introduced combinatorial challenge by S. K. Dubey and A. \v{S}t\v{c}epovi\'c in their 2021 contribution to *Combinatorics*. We reframe this problem within the domain of probability theory and employ Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate the validity of our theoretical findings.

Let $F_q$ represent a finite field where $q$ is a power of a prime $p$. We define a binomial set $B$ as a subset of $F_q$ containing elements that are $m$-th powers of $F_q$, where $m$ divides $q-1$. The study focuses on identifying the maximum possible value of $k$ such that any set $S$ of size $k$ drawn from $B$ guarantees the existence of a polynomial $f$ of degree $d$ (where $d$ is bounded by the structure of $B$) that vanishes on all points in $S$. This result is derived using a probabilistic method, which also yields a probabilistic proof for a theorem by Alon and Szabó regarding the existence of such vanishing polynomials.

We introduce a novel methodology for analyzing source code, which models the associated build process as a network capable of analysis via model checking tools such as UPPAAL. Utilizing this approach on various open-source projects, we demonstrate that the size of the generated models correlates strongly with the size of the original source code.

We introduce a framework for end-to-end optimization of metasurfaces, integrating the design process with image reconstruction to jointly minimize the loss function. This approach utilizes a neural network to model the entire imaging process, enabling direct parameterization of the meta-atoms within the metasurface structure. By training the meta-atom parameters to optimize the downstream image recovery task, we achieve metasurfaces that are specifically tuned for compressed sensing applications.

This study examines the ionization of helium atoms subjected to two-color, circularly polarized laser fields, where the field components are detuned by 1.5 ac-Stark shifts. We observe that this specific detuning creates a new resonance, which we term the "ac Stark resonance," a feature absent in single-color circular polarization scenarios. This resonance is identified as a resonance between the zeroth-order and first-order saddle points of the Coulomb potential arising from the ac-Stark effect. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the intensity of the resonance oscillates with the amplitude of the applied field. We also confirm that the resonance persists even when the two field components are detuned by 2.5 ac-Stark shifts.

Image-to-image translation is a prevalent task in computer vision, where CycleGAN has emerged as a leading method for translating images between distinct domains. However, existing CycleGAN implementations are limited to domain translation, such as converting horses to zebras, and lack the capacity to manipulate semantic attributes. To address this, we introduce a new task focused on image mixing that combines the semantic content of one image with the style of another. We propose a new method, called "CyberGAN," which utilizes a dual-styled generator capable of producing both stylized and un-stylized versions of an image. This architecture allows the system to perform both style transfer and semantic swapping simultaneously. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in both qualitative and quantitative metrics, achieving superior performance in mixing images.

Gene expression is inherently stochastic, and stochastic gene expression models are frequently employed to investigate cellular mechanisms. These models can be fitted to experimental data to estimate parameters, which are essential for predicting cellular behavior and comparing different genetic strains. This study introduces a robust and efficient framework for estimating parameters from both single-cell and time-series datasets. The approach utilizes a particle filter to generate posterior distributions for model parameters, thereby quantifying the uncertainty surrounding their values. We demonstrate the utility of this method through two case studies: a two-state switch model and a negative feedback model.

This paper introduces a data-driven semi-supervised learning framework that integrates unsupervised and supervised learning objectives within a unified neural network architecture. The approach employs a data-driven methodology to derive the objective function, ensuring the model's predictive performance remains consistent with the training data. The proposed method is validated across various classification tasks, including handwritten digit recognition, object detection, and multi-source classification. The results demonstrate that the proposed data-driven semi-supervised learning approach achieves performance comparable to leading semi-supervised techniques.

Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) is a variational quantum method designed to address combinatorial optimisation problems. This study investigates QAOA's efficacy in solving the MaxCut problem, specifically focusing on the saturation of classical performance limits. We demonstrate that QAOA can achieve this saturation by adjusting the number of quantum layers, $p$, relative to the problem size, $N$. Our findings indicate that the ratio $p/N$ must exceed a specific threshold value for QAOA to reach saturation. Furthermore, we examine the implications of these results for QAOA's application on Noisy-Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices.

Person Re-Identification (ReID) involves identifying individuals across multiple cameras. This paper reviews the state-of-the-art methodologies for ReID, with a specific focus on deep learning-based approaches. We begin by outlining the ReID task and its evaluation metrics, then proceed to a detailed analysis of current state-of-the-art techniques.

Power system research relies heavily on time series data, which can be either real-world measurements or synthetically generated. While synched datasets are widely used, they often lack the necessary characteristics of real data, such as nonlinearity, nonstationarity, and complex interdependencies. This study introduces a data-driven approach to reconstructing time series by utilizing the input-output relationships inherent within the data. We demonstrate that a neural network can effectively model these relationships, enabling the generation of an input sequence and its corresponding output. This capability allows for the creation of time series with specific features, such as a designated average value. We illustrate this method using a small-scale inverter-interfaced DC microgrid.

This paper examines the Strong Convergence of the Kaczmarz algorithm applied to resolve Variational Inequality problems. It is demonstrated that the algorithm, which incorporates a specific perturbation, converges globally to a unique solution for the problem, provided the solution set is restricted to a singleton. Furthermore, this finding extends previous work by Attouch et al. (2007) regarding the strong convergence of a proximal point algorithm featuring a monotone and Lipschitzian perturbation.

This study investigates the geometric and algebraic characteristics of isoxial Fuchsian groups, which are characterized by the property that all geodesics connecting their fixed points are geodesic lines. This property is equivalent to the group being a subgroup within a triangle group of type $(\infty, \infty, p)$ for some finite integer $p \geq 2$. We demonstrate that isoxial groups correspond precisely to those Fuchsian groups where isometric cyclic extensions of type $(p, \infty)$ exist. Additionally, we establish that the set of all such groups forms a single conjugacy class in $\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{R})$. Finally, we analyze the intersection patterns of geodesic lines originating from fixed points and derive an arithmetic characterization of these structures.

This study presents the inaugural search for the lepton flavor-violating decay $\Upsilon(3S) \rightarrow e^{\pm}\mu^{\pm}$ conducted using a dataset of 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ from the Belle experiment. The analysis yields an upper limit on the lepton flavor violation branching fraction of $< 1.0 \times 10^{-6}$ at 90% confidence level, a result that remains valid regardless of the electron identification efficiency.

This material exhibits superconductivity under high pressure, with a critical temperature ($T_c$) reaching 10.5 K at 10 GPa. Theoretical analysis suggests that the exceptionally high $T_c$ arises from strong electron-phonon coupling combined with a narrow electronic bandwidth.

Neural networks are widely recognized as effective tools for modeling the dynamics of physical systems, yet their efficacy falters when confronted with irregular datasets. This study introduces a framework that integrates Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs) with data assimilation techniques to address this gap. By leveraging neural networks to define continuous, parametric solutions to differential equations, the proposed method enables the seamless integration of Neural ODEs with noisy, incomplete, or irregularly sampled data. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness through a comprehensive analysis of linear stochastic differential equation (SDE) models, revealing that the neural architecture significantly enhances solution accuracy. Furthermore, the approach is applied to model the dynamics of a nonlinear pendulum subjected to random noise.

Object Goal Navigation (OGN) involves an agent navigating to a target specified by a textual command within an unfamiliar setting. While prior research has primarily concentrated on text-only input, this paper introduces OGN systems capable of processing mixed modality inputs comprising both text and images. We present a straightforward yet potent framework that integrates a Scene Memory Transformer with a standard encoder-decoder architecture. The system leverages the Scene Memory Transformer to identify and retain visual data of objects of interest, utilizing this memory to guide the encoder in generating scene embeddings. These embeddings facilitate the decoder in comparing environmental observations with the mixed modality input to produce navigational actions. Experimental results on the OGN-10 dataset demonstrate that our approach surpasses the performance of text-only baseline methods.

The emergence of large-scale language models (LLMs) has sparked significant interest in instruction tuning, a method that leverages data to teach models to follow commands. However, the prohibitive cost of this approach limits its scalability. To address this, we introduce OPT-IML, a scalable alternative that utilizes instruction meta-learning to fine-tune a pre-trained LLM across diverse tasks. Unlike traditional methods, OPT-IML trains on mini-batches comprising multiple tasks, enabling the model to adapt to new instructions with only a single training example. Our implementation achieves performance comparable to instruction tuning while reducing costs by approximately 90%. Additionally, we demonstrate that this framework can be applied to hundreds of tasks simultaneously, yielding substantial gains over instruction tuning for tasks within the training distribution.

This study examines how the informal learning environment of Scratch fosters participation within the programming community. Utilizing a quantitative approach, we analyzed data from 1.2 million Scratch users, evaluating their profiles, comments, and interactions alongside nine distinct indicators of Legitimate Peripheral Participation (LPP). Our findings reveal that Scratch supports multiple forms of LPP, driven by diverse motivations, evolving trajectories, and varying levels of programming proficiency. Furthermore, our results indicate that while advanced programming skills correlate with greater community engagement, they do not necessarily predict the specific type of participation adopted.

This study examines the uniform electron gas using a translationally invariant transcorrelated Hamiltonian, employing a basis set composed of plane waves entangled with the Hamiltonian. We calculate the total energy for spin-polarized systems across a wide range of densities and compare these results against established data from variational Monte Carlo simulations and coupled-cluster theory. Additionally, we compute the compressibility and chemical potential, demonstrating that both the transcorrelated approach and coupled-cluster theory yield superior accuracy compared to conventional VARIATIONAL Monte Carlo methods.

We introduce a new method for integrating location uncertainty into the training of neural networks for point clouds, specifically targeting scenarios involving physical constraints. This approach employs optimal transport to establish a probabilistic distribution over point clouds, subsequently utilizing covariance scaling to derive an uncertainty penalty for neural predictions. The resulting uncertainty metric is designed to align with the underlying probability distribution, thereby enhancing calibration. We validate this framework through experiments on a simple network performing point cloud classification and a graph convolutional network executing semantic segmentation.

Tensors are increasingly vital for modeling and analyzing high-dimensional data, yet their widespread adoption is hindered by the exponential growth of dimensions, a challenge known as the curse of dimensionality. To address this, we introduce a privacy-preserving framework that leverages randomized tensor network decomposition. This approach mitigates the curse of dimensionality by utilizing tensor network methods to break down high-dimensional data into interconnected low-rank tensors. We further develop a randomized method to generate tensor-specific keys, which are then used to fragment the data into numerous micro-batches. These micro-batches are distributed across multiple servers, where they undergo randomized private aggregation computations. This process ensures that the final result remains private, as the individual server outputs reveal no sensitive information. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the framework, including bounds on privacy, accuracy, and computational complexity. Additionally, we conduct extensive experiments using real-world datasets to demonstrate the method's effectiveness and validate our theoretical findings.

Robot learning algorithms typically require extensive training time, a process that is often unsafe to repeat in real-world settings. Consequently, researchers frequently rely on simulators to train these algorithms before deploying them on physical robots. However, the "sim-to-real" transfer problem remains a significant hurdle, as policies trained in simulation often fail to perform well in the real world. This paper introduces SafeAPT, a novel framework designed to learn robot policies that are both safe and capable of transferring effectively from simulation to reality. SafeAPT operates by training a collection of diverse policies within the simulator and subsequently selecting the most promising one for real-world deployment. Our experimental results demonstrate that SafeAPT surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in both performance and safety metrics.

This study offers an overview of the observational characteristics of jets within quasars and radio galaxies, with a specific emphasis on the physical mechanisms driving jet formation and collimation. We examine observational evidence for jet collimation and the role of magnetic fields in this process. Furthermore, we explore the energetic output of jets, including their impact on the interstellar medium and the production of X-ray cavities. We also address the issue of jet termination and the generation of radio halos and lobes. Finally, we discuss the nature of jets in low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs) and the associated observational constraints.

This study introduces a time-inhomogeneous sieve regression model tailored for nonstationary time series data. It accommodates both linear and nonlinear dynamics, including those with lagged terms, and establishes conditions for consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimator. The model's utility is demonstrated through empirical analysis of two datasets: one examining the impact of COVID-19 on US stock markets and another investigating the nonlinear relationship between US unemployment rates and the federal funds rate.

This study investigates the efficacy of neural networks compared to traditional machine learning approaches for identifying offensive speech across various languages. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of neural architectures, including Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs), and Bidirectional LSTMs, utilizing both character-level and word-level embeddings. Our findings indicate that neural models outperform traditional machine learning methods, with Bidirectional LSTM configurations utilizing word-level embeddings achieving the highest accuracy.

Functional connectivity (FC) within the human brain is a vital area of neuroscience, yet it remains difficult to quantify due to the complex, high-dimensional nature of brain activity. This study introduces a deep learning model designed to extract FC patterns from brain activity data. Our approach utilizes a graph convolutional neural network (GCNN) to capture the intrinsic topological structure of FCs, employing a self-supervised learning strategy to generate training data from raw brain activity. We further demonstrate that the model's learned FC representations can effectively predict the behavioral traits of subjects. Our findings indicate that the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in both the reconstruction of brain activity and the prediction of behaviors.

Dissipativity theory, a cornerstone of control theory, has recently been applied to optimization, where it offers a systematic approach to analyzing stability and deriving convergence rates. This paper investigates the connections between dissipativity and accelerated first-order methods, specifically Nesterov's algorithm. We establish that applying dissipativity theory to this algorithm yields two distinct interpretations: one that delivers a convergence rate and another that proves asymptotic stability. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these interpretations are mutually exclusive regarding achieving both objectives simultaneously. Finally, the work outlines the impact of dissipativity on the dynamics of Nesterov's accelerated method.

This study introduces a novel approach for boundary treatment within implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta schemes applied to hyperbolic systems featuring source terms. The method relies on the explicit upwinding of fluxes at domain boundaries, utilizing source terms derived from the method-of-lines perspective. We present a rigorous analysis of the resulting scheme, proving its consistency, stability, and convergence. Furthermore, numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the method's efficacy across various scenarios.

We introduce a novel 3D back reflector featuring a periodic silicon structure designed to enhance light absorption in thin silicon films. This back reflector is optimized to operate in conjunction with a silicon film possessing a refractive index of 3.4. Theoretical analysis indicates that the proposed structure can achieve a 200% increase in absorption for a 200 nm silicon film and a 50% increase for a 10 nm film, compared to planar designs. Furthermore, this approach is adaptable to various silicon refractive indices and can be broadly applied to other semiconductor materials.

The paper introduces credal valuation networks (CVNs), a new graphical model designed to model uncertainty in probabilistic valuation networks (PVALNs). CVNs offer advantages over PVALNs by enabling more efficient reasoning through more compact representations. We present CVNs as an extension of PVALNs where the probability distributions are replaced with sets of distributions. This change allows CVNs to encode uncertainty more succinctly, reducing the number of parameters needed compared to PVALNs. Furthermore, reasoning within CVNs can be conducted more effectively than in PVALNs by leveraging a novel algorithm called the credal junction tree algorithm. This method computes exact results in time that scales linearly with the network's size. The paper also details a sound and complete algorithm for learning CVNs from data, demonstrating that CVNs can outperform PVALNs in terms of both parameter efficiency and reasoning speed.

Recent advancements in recommender systems have demonstrated that deep learning models capable of generating user and item embeddings yield superior results compared to traditional methods. However, these models often struggle with data sparsity and the inherent complexity of accurately capturing user preferences. To address these challenges, this paper presents a probabilistic deep learning framework for top-K recommendation that integrates adaptive margin-based metric learning. This approach employs a probabilistic model to estimate the likelihood of a user interacting with specific items, thereby enhancing the model's robustness against noisy data. Additionally, a loss function is introduced to enforce a margin between embedding representations of positive and negative samples, ensuring that the model learns to clearly distinguish between items a user likes and those they do not. The proposed method was evaluated on three real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in top-K recommendation tasks.

We introduce a method for achieving efficient classification that integrates counterfactual reasoning with active learning. This approach employs a specific type of counterfactual reasoning to identify informative instances, utilizing active learning to select samples for training. Our method's performance was evaluated against state-of-the-art active learning baselines through experiments on two datasets, with results demonstrating that it outperforms these baselines.

Robust semantic mapping is crucial for enabling robots to comprehend their surroundings. To advance this field, simulators are essential for evaluating and benchmarking various mapping techniques. This paper introduces RoSmEEry, a simulator specifically designed for assessing and comparing semantic mapping algorithms. We present a simulated environment featuring a mobile robot equipped with a 3D LiDAR sensor, tasked with traversing a known map populated with objects defined by specific labels. To ensure a rigorous assessment, we developed a custom algorithmic framework that executes and compares the performance of multiple mapping strategies. Our experimental results demonstrate that RoSmEEry is a valuable resource for testing and benchmarking semantic mapping solutions.

Rikudo is a two-player impartial game where players alternate placing tiles on a graph to form a single connected component; the last player to move wins. While a prior study conjectured that determining the winner is solvable in polynomial time, we demonstrate that this decision problem is NP-complete.

Optimal transport (OT) serves as a fundamental mathematical framework for quantifying the disparity between distributions. While OT has recently gained prominence in machine learning, its computational demands often become prohibitive when dealing with massive datasets. This article provides a comprehensive overview of numerical techniques for calculating OT, specifically addressing the challenge of scaling to large data volumes. We introduce novel algorithms that leverage the inherent sparsity of transport plans and demonstrate their efficacy through extensive numerical experiments on synthetic datasets.

This paper examines the connection between the Hecke groups $G(p)$ and Ramanujan's modular equations. It establishes that for any primitive form $f$ within the space $M_{2k}(G(p))$, there exists a corresponding Ramanujan's modular equation of degree $d$ if and only if $f$ is included in the pullback set $\pi^*(g)$, where $\pi$ represents the map from $M_{2k}(G(p))$ to $M_{2k}(\SL_2(\mathbb{Z}))$ and $g$ is another primitive form. Furthermore, the study provides a fresh approach to determining the orders of degrees 5, 6, and 15 for Ramanujan's modular equations alongside other similar cases.

These findings are intended to enhance constraints on the mass distribution within the lenses and to refine the determination of the Hubble constant ($H_0$). Our analysis reveals that the lens galaxies in the TDCOSMO sample are, on average, more distant and exhibit higher velocity dispersions compared to those in the SDSS/BOSS sample. We also identify a correlation between the lens galaxies' redshifts and their velocity dispersions, a relationship that aligns with the observed correlation between stellar mass and velocity dispersion. Additionally, we find that the lens galaxies in the TDCOSMO sample are predominantly early-type galaxies, characterized by a higher fraction of ellipticals and a lower fraction of late-type galaxies than in the SDSS/BOSS group. This study introduces a difference scheme to address boundary value problems involving nonlinear $q$-fractional differential equations on the time scale. The proposed scheme's convergence order is proven to be $O(h^2)$, with numerical experiments subsequently provided to support the theoretical findings.

The phonon Hall effect (PHE) is a non-dissipative transport phenomenon occurring in non-centrosymmetric materials under acoustical and magnetic fields. While its magnitude is typically linked to sound velocity, recent findings suggest a stronger association with the topology of the crystal structure. This study demonstrates that the PHE magnitude is proportional to the scalar invariant derived from the Berry curvature of the acoustic phonon band structure. This connection is established through a theoretical framework utilizing a $k \cdot p$ Hamiltonian for acoustic phonons, which reveals that the Hall coefficient is proportional to the scalar invariant of the Berry curvature. We introduce a novel spectrometer design that integrates the nod-and-shuffle method with wide-field spectral imaging and shifted-excitation Raman difference spectroscopy (SERDS). This approach enables the simultaneous capture of Raman spectra for multiple objects within a field of view. By recording spectra at two distinct excitation wavelengths, SERDS effectively suppresses laser lines and fluorescence backgrounds, while the nod-and-shuffle mechanism allows for the detection of a wide range of objects. This system is capable of acquiring spectra from various samples concurrently, with a field of view size determined by the camera sensor's dimensions. The paper outlines the theoretical principles of this technique and presents experimental data demonstrating its application to diverse samples.

This study establishes Fejér and Levin-Stecziŋ inequalities within a matrix framework. Specifically, we examine the positive semi-definiteness of matrix sequences constructed from linear combinations of the coefficients of matrix polynomials. Our findings encompass both the matrix analogues of Fejér's theorem and a generalized version of the classical Markov-Bernstein inequality.

We investigate the validity of the averaged null energy condition (ANEC) along both null geodesics and null rays emanating from the boundary of an evaporating black hole. Our analysis reveals that while the ANEC fails for geodesics crossing the event horizon, it remains valid for non-geodesic null rays originating at the boundary. This distinction arises because the non-geodesic paths deviate from the horizon before reaching the region where the condition would be violated. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the violation of the ANEC along these paths is intrinsically linked to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy bound.

This thesis explores three distinct facets of Conformal Field Theory (CFT). The first aspect examines the 2D free boson, specifically the $\mathbb{R}^2$ CFT, and the transformations under which its correlation functions remain invariant. The second aspect focuses on the 4D $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal index, detailing its definition, properties, and a conjecture regarding its relationship to the free energy of the associated 2D theory on the three-sphere. The final aspect investigates the holographic framework of the five-dimensional Randall-Sundrum spacetime, with an emphasis on the model's conformal window.

Industrial Control Systems (ICS) are increasingly integrated into critical infrastructure, such as power grids and water treatment facilities, where they manage vital operations. This growing adoption has introduced significant cybersecurity risks, including Stuxnet, which targeted nuclear facilities, and Triton, which threatened chemical plants. To address these vulnerabilities, researchers and industry experts have developed various frameworks, including the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, to guide organizations in securing their systems. However, these frameworks often lack the practical, actionable details necessary for real-world implementation. To address this gap, this paper introduces the ICS Cybersecurity Textbook Model Maturity (ICS-CTM2), a model designed to assist organizations in evaluating and enhancing their ICS cybersecurity capabilities. By assessing an organization's current security posture against a defined maturity baseline, ICS-CTM2 identifies specific areas requiring improvement. The model is structured into three primary dimensions: Governance, Technology, and Operations. Within each dimension, specific attributes are defined, and a maturity scale ranging from Level 0 to Level 5 is applied to measure an organization's readiness. This comprehensive approach enables organizations to establish a baseline assessment, identify critical gaps, and formulate targeted improvement strategies to bolster their overall cybersecurity resilience.

This study explores multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) within a cooperative framework, specifically focusing on scenarios where agents must learn to coordinate their actions to maximize collective rewards. We introduce a novel MARL algorithm called GVR (Greedy-based Value Representation), which incorporates an agent's estimated global value into its individual policy. GVR achieves this by utilizing a greedy search to identify the specific action combination that yields the highest expected collective reward. We demonstrate that GVR is capable of learning optimal joint policies in cooperative settings, even when the underlying joint action space is exponentially large. Additionally, we show that GVR can be adapted to solve cooperative games with multiple Nash equilibria by prioritizing action combinations with higher probabilities among these equilibria. Experimental results indicate that GVR consistently outperforms existing MARL methods in terms of both sample efficiency and final performance.

Pretrained language models (PLMs) are increasingly employed across numerous natural language processing (NLP) applications, yet their potential to encode and perpetuate harmful biases remains insufficiently investigated. This paper introduces StereoSet, a straightforward benchmark designed to assess stereotypical associations within PLMs. By utilizing associations derived from the Stereotype Content Model, we evaluate PLMs on their ability to correctly classify word pairs based on characteristics like competence versus warmth. Our analysis reveals that PLMs exhibit a significant propensity to generate harmful, biased associations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that pretraining strategies, such as using word embeddings, can exacerbate these biases. Finally, we examine the impact of dataset composition and preprocessing techniques on these outcomes, offering insights to guide future research efforts.

Optimizing electrical tilt settings for base stations is a critical factor in enhancing cellular network performance. While traditional methods rely on on-policy, iterative adjustments to refine tilt configurations, this paper introduces an off-policy learning framework designed to optimize these settings. By leveraging historical data from existing networks, this approach eliminates the need for intrusive, real-world testing. The proposed method utilizes a deep reinforcement learning algorithm grounded in the Q-learning paradigm, which incorporates a deep neural network to estimate the state-action value function. We validate the efficacy of this algorithm through simulations and demonstrate that it surpasses existing on-policy, iterative optimization techniques.

A domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{C}^n$ is defined as complex symmetric when there exists a unitary involution $U$ such that the transformation $z \mapsto U(z) - c$ maps $\Omega$ onto its complement. While it was previously established that the ellipsoid $E_{\alpha,\beta} = \{ z \in \mathbb{C}^n : |\sum_{j=1}^n z_j|^2 + n\beta \leq \alpha \}$ is complex symmetric for $n \geq 2$ and $\alpha, \beta > 0$, this work extends that finding. We demonstrate that the more general domain $E_{\alpha,\beta,p} = \{ z \in \mathbb{C}^n : \sum_{j=1}^n |z_j|^p \leq \alpha + (n-1)\beta \}$ possesses the same property for $n \geq 2$, $p \geq 1$, and $\alpha, \beta > 0$.

The growing prevalence of personal data markets has sparked significant concern among the public, prompting this study to investigate how individuals respond to the concept of data trading. We conducted a survey of 1,000 participants to assess their attitudes toward data markets, the proposed data framework, and associated risks. The results indicate that while respondents perceive the current exchange of personal information as beneficial, they view the hypothetical data markets as highly problematic. Specifically, 60% of participants expressed opposition to the proposed system, citing concerns about the potential for abuse, the perception of the data as commodities, and the lack of a regulatory framework. Furthermore, the study examined laypeople's understanding of data markets and identified key factors influencing their reactions. We discovered that while respondents have a superficial grasp of the concept, they are not entirely unaware of the risks involved. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the public's aversion to data markets stems from a lack of trust in the system, which can be mitigated by implementing robust regulations and oversight mechanisms.

This study introduces a deep learning-driven approach to list sphere decoding for Faster-than-Nyquist (FTN) signaling, specifically designed to lower computational complexity. The proposed method utilizes a neural network to predict the order in which transmitted symbols are accessed during decoding. By leveraging this predicted sequence, the search process is restricted to a significantly reduced set of candidate points, effectively mitigating the high computational demands associated with FTN signaling detection. The neural network is trained using simulated FTN signals and applied to forecast decoding order sequences for subsequent detection steps. The authors evaluate the system's performance across various training configurations and compare the results with conventional sphere decoding. The findings demonstrate that this deep learning-enhanced decoder achieves performance comparable to traditional sphere decoding while drastically reducing the number of operations required.

This work examines the topological characteristics of a specific subset within the complete effect algebra of all Frink ideals of an effect algebra, focusing on how the topology relates to the underlying algebraic structure. The study demonstrates that this subset forms a $T_0$ space that is compact when the Frink ideal algebra corresponds to an effect algebra possessing a top element; notably, it proves the topological structure remains equivalent to the effect algebra ordered by its partial order, provided the Frink ideal algebra corresponds to an effect algebra with a complete lattice structure. Under the additional assumption that the effect algebra satisfies the distributive property, it is shown that the Frink ideal algebra retains the same topological structure as the effect algebra ordered by its partial order, with both structures remaining equivalent whenever the effect algebra forms a complete lattice.

Data augmentation is a common technique for enhancing the generalization of machine learning models, particularly in computer vision. However, conventional augmentation strategies often fail to adequately capture the essential characteristics of input data. To address this, we introduce a novel saliency-guided augmentation method called SaliencyMix. SaliencyMix identifies the most informative regions within images and performs mixing operations specifically on these areas to generate diverse training samples. This approach is straightforward to implement and requires no additional parameters. Extensive experiments across various tasks and datasets demonstrate that SaliencyMix achieves significant performance improvements when used as a standalone method or integrated with existing state-of-the-art models.
We examine two distinct families of non-negative unitary traces defined on the infinite-dimensional Iwahori-Hecke algebra associated with SL(2).

Intrinsic alignments (IA) of galaxies are a significant source of systematic error in weak lensing studies, yet their impact on cosmological constraints remains uncertain. This study examines how IA affects the measurement of cosmological parameters within the context of $\Lambda$CDM and modified gravity (specifically Horndeski) theories. We utilize a combined analysis of cosmic shear and intrinsic alignments, employing the non-linear matter power spectrum predicted by the Halofit algorithm. Our results indicate that incorporating both cosmic shear and IA data yields robust constraints on cosmological parameters, even when the IA signal is modeled with limited precision. Furthermore, we find that accounting for IA is essential for obtaining unbiased cosmological estimates from cosmic shear analyses.

By applying this approach to diverse nanoparticle shapes, we derive a universal melting temperature formula that accounts for shape variations. This formula is expressed as a function of the inverse squared radius and a specific shape factor, which is defined by the ratio of surface area to volume.

We introduce a novel approach to the flavor problem in particle physics, which is uniquely characterized by a geometric symmetry known as the "tetrahedron of flavors." This framework offers a fresh perspective on the classification of Standard Model fermions, the understanding of their mixing patterns, and the analysis of their CP violation. By employing a coordinate system based on the tetrahedron, we demonstrate that the three families of leptons can be organized into three distinct, non-intersecting sets, each defined by a specific common value. Furthermore, we show that this group-theoretic structure is isomorphic to the mathematical group $S_4$, which describes the symmetries of a tetrahedron.

This study establishes novel relations for $(h,q)$-Genocchi numbers and polynomials by employing the fermionic $p$-adic measure on the $p$-adic integers alongside the $q$-exponential function. Furthermore, we derive a novel formula expressing the weighted $p$-adic zeta function in terms of $(h,q)$-Genocchi numbers.

Estimating the long-term impacts of treatments is essential for designing effective policies, yet these effects are notoriously difficult to quantify because data is sparse, outcomes are delayed, and confounding factors remain unmeasured. This paper introduces a reinforcement learning approach designed to estimate the long-term effects of treatments on continuous variables, even when the data is limited. The method utilizes a novel, continuous-state, Markovian reward function to estimate long-term treatment impacts, a framework that is proven to converge to the true effect as the sample size grows. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the proposed estimator achieves a faster convergence rate compared to existing methods, particularly in scenarios with scarce data.

Case-control studies are frequently employed to investigate risk factors for rare diseases, yet they often rely on participant memory for exposure data. This reliance introduces recall bias, as participants' tendency to misremember varies based on their case or control status as well as their actual exposure level. While prior research has addressed this issue using logistic regression, it fails to account for the causal link between true exposure and case/control status. This paper instead proposes a novel method grounded in causal inference. We introduce a new parameter that quantifies the extent of the causal effect of exposure on case/control status, enabling a more accurate assessment of the association between observed exposure and disease status. We evaluate this approach using both simulated data and analysis of the National Collaborating Centre for Nursing and Midwifery Quality Improvement's National Audit of Midwifery data. Our findings indicate that incorporating the causal effect parameter substantially alters the estimated association between observed exposure and case/control status, particularly when the magnitude of this effect is substantial.

Autoencoders are a prevalent class of generative models that encode input data into a lower-dimensional latent representation and subsequently reconstruct the original data from that encoding. While standard implementations use non-linear, non-invertible layers to achieve dimensionality reduction, this study explores an alternative approach utilizing invertible architectures. By incorporating invertible layers, we can derive the exact log-likelihood of the training data, a metric that is otherwise inaccessible with conventional autoencoders. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework for constructing invertible autoencoders and evaluates their performance on various image datasets. Our results indicate that invertible autoencoders can match the reconstruction quality of traditional models while offering the advantage of exact likelihood computation.

Smart cities are designed to enhance the quality of urban life by leveraging data from various sensors and devices. While existing smart city data analysis tools typically focus on identifying statistical correlations between attributes, they fail to account for correlations within the attribute values themselves. This study introduces a novel approach to visualize correlations among attribute values, thereby supporting the discovery of correlated attribute patterns. This method comprises two phases: first, a data-driven strategy for identifying correlated attribute patterns, and second, a visualization technique for presenting these patterns. The visualization technique operates in two steps: initially, it employs a dimensionality reduction method to generate an attribute map, and subsequently, it displays the correlated attribute patterns within this map. The pattern discovery phase utilizes a graph-based algorithm to locate correlated attribute patterns, while the visualization employs a map-based approach to present these patterns effectively. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the analysis of smart city data.

This study introduces geometric multigrid preconditioners tailored for discretized hyperbolic diffusion problems (HDG-P0) applied to reaction-diffusion equations and generalized Stokes systems. By leveraging the mixed formulation of these problems, the approach employs a Raviart-Thomas finite element scheme on rectangular grids. The preconditioner's efficiency relies on a coarse-fine coupling strategy that bridges different finite element spaces across levels. Specifically, the diffusive component is approximated using a low-order discretization on the coarse grid, whereas the remaining terms are handled via a high-order discretization. The resulting preconditioner is proven to be computationally efficient, with its cost scaling at a rate lower than that of the underlying linear system solver.

This paper introduces a Bayesian sensitivity analysis method for handling missing data, specifically addressing scenarios where the Missing at Random (MAR) assumption cannot be justified. We utilize the "E-value," a recently proposed metric for evaluating unmeasured confounding, to quantify the magnitude of confounding required to overturn a study conclusion. By integrating this metric with Bayesian inference, we construct a flexible framework that enables researchers to assess robustness to the extent of potential confounding. We demonstrate the application of this approach through a simulation study and a real-world analysis of the relationship between statin use and cardiovascular disease mortality in the Swedish SWEDEHEART registry.

Multivariate crossover trials frequently employ a repeated measures design, where participants alternate between two treatment conditions across two periods. In this setup, the first period involves one treatment, while the second involves either the other or the same one, depending on the randomization. A significant challenge in these studies is missing data, which can stem from protocol violations, adverse events, or logistical failures, potentially introducing bias if not properly managed. This paper examines three distinct missing data scenarios: missing baseline measurements, missing post-treatment outcomes, and missing treatment assignments. We introduce a likelihood-based approach to handle these issues, demonstrating that it yields valid inferences even when data are missing not at random (MNAR). Our method remains robust under the assumption that MNAR data arise from a combination of unobserved factors and observed covariates. We validate our approach through simulation studies and apply it to real-world data from a crossover trial evaluating the effects of a specific drug on blood pressure.

We demonstrate that the $A_n$-graph associated with an $(n+1)$-category equipped with weak monoidal structures can be substituted by an analogous construction for strictly associative $(n-2)$-monoidal $(n-1)$-categories.

DRAM is a critical component of modern computing, yet its performance is often bottlenecked by the inherent limitations of DRAM chips. To address this, recent research has explored using reconfigurable logic to create custom DRAM functionality, yet such approaches are costly and offer limited flexibility. In response, this paper introduces CODIC, a low-cost, custom DRAM interface substrate designed to enable flexible, user-specific in-DRAM functionality. CODIC is built upon a low-cost FPGA and a custom DRAM interface, allowing users to program the FPGA to create bespoke DRAM interfaces. By utilizing a modular architecture, CODIC supports the development of various DRAM interfaces, including those for specific applications, custom DRAM controllers, and even educational tools. Additionally, CODIC's small footprint and low power consumption make it suitable for integration into existing computing systems.

This is the second installment of a two-part series examining the application of functional programming within the management and orchestration of virtualized network resources. While the initial part highlighted the advantages functional programming offers for network management, this part explores the challenges inherent in evolving network systems alongside the principles guiding their design.

The toric code serves as a foundational model for topological quantum error correction, offering a framework to investigate key challenges in building a fault-tolerant quantum computer. This research examines the viability of implementing two-qubit and multi-qubit gates within the toric code, specifically focusing on the number of T gates necessary for various operations. We demonstrate that while two-qubit gates can be executed using only a constant amount of T gates, performing multi-qubit gates demands an exponential number of T gates in relation to qubit count. This finding underscores the trade-off between the complexity of quantum gates and the resources required for their implementation within a topological quantum computing architecture.

OPUS is a job control system designed to manage observational requests for the Virtual Observatory (VO). It is being developed by the INAF-TO observatories to support the ESO-ALMA joint project, specifically the ALMA Large Program 12A, which focuses on studying the interstellar medium. The system allows users to submit observational requests that are automatically converted into ESO and ALMA standard formats. A key feature of OPUS is its ability to retrieve data from various sources, including local databases and the VO through the VO-standardized Client Application Protocol (VOCAP). Additionally, the system includes a web interface for submitting requests and monitoring their status, as well as a graphical user interface (GUI) for analyzing data cubes and spectral data.

This paper outlines a method for embedding a game-based learning module to teach wireless communication concepts, utilizing the advanced network capabilities of modern smartphones. The proposed module is designed to be adaptable for integration into various educational settings, ranging from high school curricula to university engineering programs. It focuses on key wireless communication principles, specifically 3D spatial positioning and the measurement of Received Signal Strength (RSS). The module's effectiveness was assessed through a user study involving 24 undergraduate students, with results indicating that the gamified approach significantly enhanced their understanding of wireless communication concepts.

Ozone (O$_3$) serves as a potent proxy for molecular oxygen (O$_2$) in exoplanetary atmospheres, given that O$_2$ is the primary driver of O$_3$ production. This study investigates the O$_2$-O$_3$ relationship within Earth-like exoplanets, specifically examining how stellar flux and atmospheric composition influence the ozone-to-oxygen ratio. We find that the O$_2$-O$_3$ ratio is governed by two main factors: the host star's emission spectrum and the atmospheric photochemistry. While the ratio remains relatively stable across varying atmospheric compositions, it is highly sensitive to stellar flux. Specifically, for Earth-like planets orbiting Sun-like stars, the O$_2$-O$_3$ ratio is approximately 10$^5$, a value that can vary by a factor of 100 depending on the host star's flux. Consequently, ozone absorption features are generally more detectable than those of O$_2$ in transmission spectra, though this ratio can be further modulated by atmospheric composition. We also examine the potential for O$_2$ and O$_3$ to coexist in an Earth-like atmosphere with a hydrogen-dominated background. Our results indicate that such a scenario is unlikely, as the O$_2$-O$_3$ ratio would be significantly lower than 10$^5$ in hydrogen-dominated atmospheres.

We investigate surface currents within a semi-infinite version of the 3D cubic Hofstadter model, characterized by a uniform magnetic field applied along the $z$-axis. Our findings indicate that surface currents exist in the energy bands of the bulk that are gapped, a phenomenon occurring regardless of the specific magnetic flux magnitude. These surface currents are robust against perturbations that maintain the model's chiral symmetry. We identify two distinct categories of surface currents: those found in bands with a nonzero bulk Chern number and those present in bands with a zero bulk Chern number.

Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (MNMT) has recently achieved significant advancements, yet its application within specialized fields like healthcare remains underexplored. This study investigates how domain- and task-adaptation of multilingual translation models impact their effectiveness in medical contexts. We evaluate both general-purpose and specialized models across diverse healthcare domains, focusing on the specific effects of adaptation on performance. Our findings indicate that while general-purpose models struggle to deliver clinically relevant results, medical domain-specific multilingual models exhibit superior performance.

This study investigates the formation of modified ion-acoustic (MIA) solitary waves and shocks within a plasma environment comprising nonthermal electrons, positively charged dust, and a mixture of cold and hot ions. By employing a reductive perturbation technique, we derive a Korteweg-de Vries-Zakharov-Kuznetsov (MKdVZ) equation applicable to this specific plasma configuration. The analysis demonstrates that the derived MIAWs possess a dual nature, exhibiting either compressive or rarefactive characteristics, which depends on the ratio of ion temperatures and the electron nonthermal parameter. Furthermore, we determine the critical Mach number and confirm that modified ion-acoustic shock waves can exist within this plasma system.

This study introduces ContextAware SentencePretraining (CASP) to enhance sentence embeddings for multi-lingual dense retrieval. CASP employs a novel, context-aware pretraining strategy that utilizes unstructured paragraphs as masks to generate masked representations, thereby enabling the model to learn representations that incorporate surrounding context. Evaluated on the MS MARCO and TREC datasets, the CASP-enhanced SentenceBERT model demonstrates significant performance gains. Additionally, the approach exhibits strong adaptability when fine-tuned on specific domains, such as the medical MedMCPlus dataset. These outcomes underscore the effectiveness of pretraining sentence embeddings with context-rich information.

Recent advances in multimodal learning have predominantly focused on leveraging complementary information from different modalities to enhance performance. However, existing multimodal datasets often exhibit inherent modality imbalance, where certain modalities are more prevalent than others. This bias can lead to models that over-rely on dominant modalities, thereby compromising their effectiveness in scenarios involving missing data. To address this, we introduce Prototypical Modality Rebalance (PMR), a novel training framework designed to optimize collaboration between modalities. PMR achieves two key objectives: first, it actively mitigates modularity imbalance by generating synthetic samples to balance the distribution; second, it fosters effective multimodal synergy by training the model to identify the most suitable modality for a given input. Empirical results demonstrate that PMR significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across various tasks, including image classification, action recognition, and audio-visual question answering.

This study examines the transport theory of a gas of massless particles interacting via a vector field, with the dynamics of said field governed by classical equations. We establish a rigorous framework for the classical system, proving the existence of local solutions to the associated coupled transport equations when the data are smooth. Subsequently, we investigate the system's behavior under linearization at thermodynamic equilibrium, revealing that perturbations evolve according to a linear kinetic equation featuring a non-local term derived from the interaction's propagation. Our findings demonstrate that, in the limit where interaction speeds approach infinity relative to particle speeds, these equations align with a linearized kinetic framework. This specific form includes a local first-order term representing advection caused by a classical force, alongside a relaxation term. Finally, we analyze the system's linearized stability within this high-velocity coupling regime.

This study introduces a hybrid tensor-train network (TTN) designed to integrate the superior accuracy of deep neural networks (DNNs) with the efficiency of TTNs. The proposed architecture merges a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a TTN, utilizing the CNN to extract high-level features and the TTN to model long-range dependencies. To optimize the hybrid model, we developed a novel tensor-train decomposition algorithm that incorporates the CNN output as input. This approach significantly reduces computational costs and memory usage while maintaining high modeling accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that this hybrid method surpasses the performance of standalone TTNs and DNNs, achieving a 29.1% reduction in word error rate (WER) and a 20.1% reduction in phoneme recognition error rate (PRR) on the TIMIT dataset.

This study introduces a method for constructing quantum-jump trajectories applicable to systems governed by a master equation. The technique enables the incorporation of specific physical insights, such as the identification of distinct quantum dot subpopulations or the classification of photon emissions by wavelength, directly into trajectory generation. We demonstrate the approach using a quantum dot ensemble where emission rates vary across subunits. Our findings indicate that the proposed methodology is broadly applicable to any quantum system described by a master equation.

This study investigates the impact of plasmonic aluminum (Al) nanoparticles with varying geometries on the optical absorption within thin-film silicon solar cells. The analysis covers nanoparticles in shapes of cubes, spheres, and octahedra, with dimensions ranging from 10 to 100 nm. The findings indicate that the absorption boost is most significant when using octahedral Al nanoparticles sized between 20 and 50 nm, surpassing the performance of spherical and cubic particles of equivalent scale. This enhanced performance is attributed to the superior optical properties of octahedral Al nanoparticles, which facilitate greater energy transfer from the adjacent active layer to the metal.

We introduce a logic designed to capture deterministic polynomial time (PTIME) within databases, extending First-Order Logic (FOL) with a choice operator and a formula selection feature. This logic demonstrates the following capabilities in our work: (i) it successfully defines every query expressible in deterministic PTIME; (ii) it successfully defines every query computable via FOL combined with the choice operator; (iii) it successfully defines every query computable via FOL combined with a generalized fixpoint operator that selects formulas. These results are achieved through a new evaluation method that assesses queries on databases augmented with auxiliary relations, where the number of such relations and their cardinality are restricted by polynomial bounds.

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks are extensively utilized in video recognition tasks, yet their computational demands and memory requirements are substantial, making them difficult to deploy on energy-constrained edge devices. To address this, we introduce a hierarchical hierarchical tensor decomposition (HHTD) algorithm designed to reduce the complexity of LSTM networks. Our approach involves decomposing the recurrent weights into a hierarchical structure of low-rank tensors, alongside a specialized algorithm for efficient tensor multiplication. We further developed a hierarchical tensor-based LSTM (HT-LSTM) architecture and co-designed a hardware accelerator for HT-LSTM execution. Experimental results indicate that HT-LSTM achieves a 99.0% top-1 accuracy on the Kinetics-400 dataset, matching the performance of standard LSTM networks. Additionally, our HT-LSTM hardware accelerator demonstrates a 90% reduction in energy consumption compared to a conventional systolic array implementation.

The MAVLink protocol serves as a critical communication standard for unmanned aerial systems, facilitating data exchange between vehicles and ground control stations. However, its current design lacks essential security features, leaving the system vulnerable to various attacks. This paper introduces a security solution that enhances MAVLink by integrating encryption and authentication. It proposes a novel protocol that implements the AES-GCM authenticated encryption scheme, which provides robust confidentiality and integrity guarantees. Furthermore, the study includes a comprehensive security analysis of the proposed protocol and a discussion on the practical challenges involved in deploying this system in real-world scenarios.

This paper introduces Kollaps, a decentralized and dynamic system for emulating network topologies. Kollaps enables the creation of flexible, decentralized, and dynamic topological models, where each node operates independently without relying on a central authority. It achieves this by allowing nodes to exchange messages over the Internet, thereby supporting the creation of topologies that span the global network. Additionally, the paper details the implementation of the Kollaps system and evaluates its performance through experiments.

This article outlines an alternative approach to comprehending the Newman-Penrose formalism for four-dimensional spacetime, specifically regarding its application to null geodesics. By leveraging the correspondence between complex projective spinors and null directions, the study examines how vector fields and their covariant derivatives transform across different frames. The resulting derivations lead to a set of differential equations describing the holonomy of geodesics, which are expressed entirely within twistors language. These findings demonstrate that the geometric data characterizing null geodesics can be represented using four complex functions, thereby offering a novel derivation of the Newman-Penrose mapping.

This study details the design and construction of a novel muon detector developed for the 100 m$^2$ underground tomography experiment at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory in Italy. The setup comprises 16 silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readout photodiodes, each coupled with a 3 cm thick scintillator bar, arranged in a 4 $\times$ 4 grid to form a 30 $\times$ 30 cm$^2$ module. The entire assembly, consisting of 16 such modules, measures 1.6 m$^2$ in area and was mounted on a 1.6 m long aluminum beam. The system's performance was evaluated using a 100 m$^2$ underground tomography experiment at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory in Italy. This paper presents a parsing algorithm designed for regular languages and regular expressions, utilizing a parsing expression grammar. We call this method PEG-GLL, which serves as a deterministic variant of the well-established GLL algorithm.

This study examines the emission of Cherenkov radiation by massless particles within a thermal medium, focusing on a scenario where Lorentz symmetry is broken. Under such conditions, massless particles may acquire a vacuum refractive index differing from that of the hot medium. Consequently, these particles can emit a photon while traversing the medium, a process known as vacuum Cherenkov radiation. The analysis reveals that this emission rate increases with temperature, potentially becoming significant at high temperatures.

Although neural models excel at predicting text, their performance degrades when evaluated on longer contexts, and their internal decision-making processes remain opaque. This study investigates whether integrating a meta-learning module can enhance tracking capabilities for these models. We introduce a novel method that utilizes a generative model to forecast the internal states of a target model, thereby enabling precise predictions of its outputs. This approach is validated by successfully tracking a state-of-the-art language model across various domains. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the internal state of this generative model can serve as a reliable proxy for the original target model's state, offering a means to interpret its behavior.

We introduce a novel approach for estimating the 3D orientation of objects by utilizing a single image paired with the object's rotational trajectory. This trajectory is generated by an accidental encounter, such as a robotic camera capturing a freely rotating object on a turntable. This dynamic process is modeled as a joint inference task involving the object's pose and the turntable's rotation angle, solved using a unified deep neural network. This system simultaneously encodes the 3D pose from the camera view and the rotation angle from the movement data. Our method demonstrates robust performance across various real-world scenarios involving diverse, freely rotating objects, including those on industrial turntables. Furthermore, we establish a new benchmark for evaluating 3D orientation estimation and validate our method against existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study investigates Andreev bound states (ABSs) within a quantum dot connected to two superconducting leads. We demonstrate that the crossed Andreev reflection (CAR) process is tunable through the application of an external magnetic field, which shifts the ABSs in energy. This energy shift is driven by the magnetic field-induced splitting of the ABSs in the direction of the field. We further analyze the specific transport mechanisms, identifying two distinct processes: the elastic co-tunneling (ECT) process and the CAR process. Both are examined in detail, revealing that the ECT process is characterized by the tunneling of an electron from one superconducting lead to the quantum dot, accompanied by the simultaneous tunneling of a hole from the opposite lead to the dot. In contrast, the CAR process involves the electron entering the dot from one lead while the hole exits to the other. We also examine the temperature dependence of the CAR and ECT processes. Our findings indicate that the ECT process is significantly more robust against temperature variations than the CAR process.
